definitions.meaning: a rough here is a street ruffian, the sense of the Parisian underworld word for a thug
a member of a Native American people of the south-west United States

explanation.surface: Someone asks what a tough life a Native American led.
explanation.definitionFit: Paris borrowed the tribe's name for its street hooligans, so both a tribesman and a thug carry it.

parts.note: the governess in The Importance of Being Earnest shares her name with a glass block that bends light

explanation.surface: A question about an unruly young woman in Oscar Wilde.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refractory' looks like 'stubborn'; here it means bending light. The governess in Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest bears the name of the glass block that refracts it.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilde's governess has the name of the glass solid that splits light into a spectrum.

clue.text: The tribe seek to return under many a brave leader

indicators.note: under places the reversed word below the others in this down answer

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, many
a hero is a brave leader

indicators.note: to return means seek is read backwards

explanation.surface: Native Americans go back to look for a courageous chief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to return' turns SEEK into KEES, and 'under' puts it below C and HERO in the down light.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cherokee are a Native American people of the south-eastern United States.

clue.text: Coming, do they happen to have the sun behind them?

definitions.text: Coming, do they happen to have the sun behind them?

parts.words: Coming, do they happen to have the sun behind them
parts.note: plays on the proverb that coming things cast their shadows before, which happens only with the light behind

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether approaching things are lit from behind.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'coming events cast their shadows before' implies the sun is behind them; 'happen' hints that these are happenings.
explanation.definitionFit: Happenings are occurrences, and the proverb says coming ones cast shadows ahead.

parts.note: Shakespeare's Romeo married into disaster, and the Wild West heroine called Jane carries the same word as her nickname

explanation.surface: A question about whom Romeo married, offering a woman named Jane.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo's secret marriage to Juliet ended in double death, a disaster; Martha Jane Canary of the American frontier was known by that same word for disaster.
explanation.definitionFit: A disaster is the misfortune Romeo wed, and the frontierswoman Martha Canary was nicknamed for it.

clue.text: His a star place in history

definitions.text: His a star place in history

parts.words: His a star place in history
parts.note: the Paris square named for a star, Place de l'Etoile, was renamed after the French wartime leader

explanation.surface: A celebrity has earned his place in the history books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'star' means a celebrity in the surface; the Place de l'Etoile (star square) in Paris was renamed for the general in 1970, so his name is on a star place.
explanation.definitionFit: The Free French leader and president gave his name to the Paris square once called the star.

clue.text: Get a pound up and clear out from the feast

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for a pound, from Latin libra
taken as written

indicators.note: out says the letters of clear are put out of order

explanation.surface: Earn some money and get away from the banquet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clear out' looks like 'leave'; 'out' shuffles CLEAR into ERCAL.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman fertility festival of February, held on the Lupercal hill, carried this name.

definitions.meaning: the Latin verb for 'you prefer' in the second person singular
an old name for the song thrush

explanation.surface: Someone is asked whether they'd rather have an Italian songbird.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin for 'thou dost prefer' is the same word as the old name for the song thrush.

clue.text: The detail, under Edward, rolled up

indicators.note: detail is read as de-tail, cutting the last letter off the

parts.note: taken as written
Ed is a short form of Edward

explanation.surface: The particulars, during the reign of King Edward, were wrapped up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detail' looks like a noun; read as de-tail it docks THE to TH.
explanation.definitionFit: A storm that boomed and rumbled across the sky is said to have rolled up.

clue.text: Generally helpful, he has the odd idea to abscond

indicators.note: odd suggests the word idea is set out in a strange new order

parts.note: to abscond is to run off, to decamp

explanation.surface: A kindly man with a strange notion of running away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Generally helpful' means helpful to a general, not helpful in general. 'odd' shuffles IDEA into AIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: A military assistant attends a senior officer, so he is helpful to a general.

indicators.note: is spoken says the German word is pronounced, and its sound is what goes in the grid

parts.note: the German word for where is wo, pronounced with a V sound

explanation.surface: A question about which Swiss district uses the German language.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks for a German-speaking canton, but this canton speaks French: German 'wo' (where) is said 'voh', the sound of the canton's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Vaud is one of the Swiss cantons, around Lausanne on Lake Geneva.

parts.note: recalls the dying queen's line in Shakespeare, 'I have ___ longings in me'

explanation.surface: A remark on what the Egyptian queen yearned for.
explanation.walkthrough: In Antony and Cleopatra the queen, about to die, says 'Give me my robe, put on my crown; I have immortal longings in me.'
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Cleopatra describes her wish for undying life with this word for deathless.

clue.text: More's ideal land in which to live

indicators.note: the land the solver wants is the stretch of letters lying in the words that follow

explanation.surface: Thomas More's Utopia is an ideal country to settle in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More's ideal land' calls up Thomas More's Utopia, but the letters run across MORE'S IDEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwell somewhere permanently is to live there.

clue.text: This is the French version of Manhattan for instance

parts.note: le is the French masculine word for the

explanation.surface: A French translation of a New York borough is offered.
explanation.definitionFit: Manhattan is an island, and isle is a poetic word for an island.

parts.note: brandling read as brand plus ling: an old word for a blade and a cod-like fish

explanation.surface: A request for the meaning of an angler's worm.
explanation.walkthrough: A brandling is really a worm, but split it: BRAND is an old word for a blade and LING a sea fish, so it defines a blade-fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Brand (a blade) plus ling (a fish) together give the big fish with a long bill.

definitions.note: read as norm is, the definition naming the answer as a norm

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way
taken as written
Rd is the abbreviation for road, a way

explanation.surface: Norm keeps on going his own way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Norm' looks like a man's name; it is the definition, with 's for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A norm is the accepted level or benchmark, the usual measure.

clue.text: Horrible murder ? Time for detention charge

indicators.note: horrible suggests murder is mangled into a new order

parts.note: an age is a long time

explanation.surface: An awful killing, then it is time to charge someone and hold them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horrible' turns MURDER into DEMURR; 'detention' means a ship held up, not a prisoner.
explanation.definitionFit: Demurrage is the fee paid when a ship or wagon is kept beyond the agreed time.

clue.text: Annabel Lee's creator starts to describe his work

definitions.text: Annabel Lee's creator starts to describe his work

parts.words: Annabel Lee's creator starts to describe his work
parts.note: the American writer of the poem Annabel Lee is Poe, whose name begins the adjective for his verse

explanation.surface: The author of the poem Annabel Lee begins to explain his writing.
explanation.walkthrough: Edgar Allan Poe wrote the poem Annabel Lee; his surname is how the answer starts, and the whole word describes his verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Verse is the work of a poet, and the adjective for it applies to Poe's lines.

definitions.meaning: an old mixed drink of gin added to beer or porter
a pet's snout is said to be cool and damp when the animal is well

explanation.surface: Gin mixed with beer is good for you if served chilled.
explanation.definitionFit: The old drink of gin in beer has this name, and folk wisdom says a hound's snout is cold when it is well.

indicators.note: say signals that the words before it are to be heard rather than read

parts.note: to have cut grass is to have mowed it

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether trimming the lawn is the right method.
explanation.definitionFit: A mode is a manner or method, a way of doing something.

parts.note: the eighteenth-century English painter famous for his pictures of horses

explanation.surface: A rider named George.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horseman' suggests a rider; George Stubbs was the English painter best known for his horse portraits, such as Whistlejacket.
explanation.definitionFit: George Stubbs painted and anatomised horses, making him a horse painter rather than a rider.

clue.text: Being skilful, is entitled to drive so abroad

definitions.meaning: being deft or clever with the hands

definitions.text: is entitled to drive so abroad
definitions.meaning: French a droit means having the right, and a droite, on the right, is the side the French drive on

explanation.surface: A capable driver may legally take the wheel overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as French, 'a droit' means has the right (is entitled), and 'a droite', to the right, is how traffic drives on the Continent.
explanation.definitionFit: Being deft and dexterous is being skilful, and the French phrase means having the right, or on the right.

parts.note: a bulb vegetable made of many layered skins, a head in the greengrocer's sense

explanation.surface: A question about a shaven-headed youth with many layers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'skin-head' calls up a shaven youth; read it as a head (bulb) made of many skins, the layered vegetable.
explanation.definitionFit: The bulb vegetable is built of many papery skins in layers.

clue.text: Skaters go wild about one star

indicators.note: about means the scrambled skaters goes round the letter for one
go wild means the letters of skaters run loose into a new order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Ice skaters run riot around a single celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go wild' shuffles SKATERS into ASTERSK, and 'about' puts I inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An asterisk is the printed star symbol used to flag a footnote.

indicators.note: perhaps suggests waste may be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Is the effort put in just squandered work?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waste of labour' reads as a phrase; 'Perhaps' shuffles WASTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Toil and hard work are labour, the effort that brings a person out in perspiration.

indicators.note: return means the conditions are read backwards

parts.note: two ifs, two conditions

explanation.surface: Someone asks on what terms she will come back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conditions' gives two IFs; 'return' turns IFIF round.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's pet name stands for her, the female person meant.

clue.text: Had a famous time to mark the occasion

definitions.text: Had a famous time to mark the occasion

parts.words: Had a famous time to mark the occasion
parts.note: both the word for renowned and the word for having held a party in honour of an event

explanation.surface: Someone enjoyed a splendid party in honour of an event.
explanation.walkthrough: The one word means both famous and having marked an occasion with festivities, and the clue runs both senses together.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means renowned, and also having marked an event with festivities.

clue.text: Oddly enough a leech takes in nothing material

indicators.note: takes in means the scrambled leech holds the word for nothing inside it
oddly enough says the letters of leech are to be arranged strangely

parts.note: nil means nothing

explanation.surface: Strangely, a bloodsucker eats nothing physical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly enough' makes CHELE from LEECH, and 'takes in' puts NIL inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Chenille is a velvety tufted yarn and the fabric made from it, a material.

parts.note: rest here is a nap, and Spain's custom is the afternoon one

explanation.surface: A remark about the remainder of the Spanish nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rest' looks like 'remainder'; it means a nap, the Spanish afternoon sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spanish afternoon nap is taken in the heat after lunch.
